speaker_notes.note: The student cites the novel 'Silence' as an analogy for contingent will under persecution; the ASR garbles parts of the reference but the comparison is intelligible.

interactions.summary: Students first define absolute will as unconditional fidelity to God and contingent will as surrender under threat, then suggest a second contrast between imagination-driven story and reasoning-driven comparison of outcomes.

Jiang reframes the question through absolute versus relative morality, students compare the issue to persecuted priests in 'Silence' and to reality-constrained human will versus God's love in us, and Jiang keeps pressing for a simpler formulation.

claims.claim: One student defines absolute will as loving God no matter what, while contingent will appears when love yields because someone threatens death.
Another student says absolute will comes from imagination and one's own story, while contingent will comes from reasoning, logic, and outcome comparison.
Jiang tests the will distinction by comparing it to absolute versus relative morality, pushing the class to see the issue as more than a vocabulary difference.
A student links contingent will to tragic compromise in 'Silence,' where priests abandon a visible vocation to protect Japanese believers from greater harm.
Another student says contingent will is constrained by reality, whereas absolute will is always there and is basically God or the divine love placed in us.
Jiang remains dissatisfied with each formulation because he is pushing toward a sharper, simpler account of the distinction than the class has yet given.

signature_moments.moment: The first student answer turns contingent will into the instant when fidelity to God buckles because someone says love God and I will kill you.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if you love god i'll kill you
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the cleanest fear-pressure version of the distinction before Jiang supplies his own synthesis.

signature_moments.moment: A student tries a more imaginative split by saying absolute will belongs to story and imagination while contingent will belongs to reasoning and outcome calculation.
signature_moments.source_phrase: absolute will comes from imagination it comes from your own story
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It surfaces a live classroom attempt to tie will to narrative identity rather than only moral pressure.

signature_moments.moment: The class imports 'Silence' to describe the priest who breaks form to spare others from a worse persecution.
signature_moments.source_phrase: because i don't want more harm to be done
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It widens the packet beyond Dante and shows the exact type of moral emergency Jiang wants the distinction to explain.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's prompt analogy for absolute will: the kind of moral claim that does not bend with circumstances.
The circumstance-sensitive moral logic Jiang uses as a comparison point for contingent will and harm-reduction reasoning.

chronology_notes.note: This packet is mostly exploratory. The class cycles through several candidate definitions for absolute and contingent will, while Jiang keeps the distinction open and presses toward a more reduced explanation in the next packet.

uncertainty_notes.note: The ASR is rough in the student's 'Silence' example, but the intended point is a compromise made to prevent greater harm to persecuted believers.
